request.channel_voice_profile: Clear, practical and conversational. Address the viewer directly; use complete sentences, explain unfamiliar terms, avoid hype, unsupported claims and invented personal experience.
request.topic: Git staging versus committing: choose what goes into one snapshot
request.angle: Teach a beginner with two changed files to commit only one. Show status, stage a named example file, inspect the staged diff, commit, then check what remains. Explain the index/working-tree distinction. Use hypothetical labels only; do not imply Git was executed.

notes: Use a hypothetical repository with app.py and notes.txt changed. The example paths are illustrative, not source facts or observed output.

Show git status, git add app.py, git diff --cached, git commit -m "Update app", and git status again as an intentional sequence. Do not fabricate command output, commit IDs, or an actual execution result.
Explain that staging app.py does not stage notes.txt and that the basic git commit form records the staged contents.
Use concrete visual contrast between working tree, index and commit. Reserve the bottom of the portrait frame for captions.

claims.text: git status reports changes staged for the next commit separately from unstaged working-tree changes.
git add followed by a path adds that file's current contents to the index, which is the staging area for preparing the next commit.
git diff --cached shows changes staged for the next commit compared with HEAD.
In its basic form, git commit with a message records the current index contents and excludes unstaged working-tree changes.

script_sections.narration: Before you commit two changed files, choose exactly what Git records. Here is the safe sequence.
Start with git status. It separates changes staged for the next commit from unstaged working-tree changes.
Now use git add app.py. This copies app.py’s current contents into the index, Git’s staging area; notes.txt stays unstaged.
Check git diff --cached. It shows what the index currently holds for the next commit compared with HEAD.
Then run git commit -m “Update app”. In this basic form, Git records the index, not unstaged working-tree changes.
Finish with git status. You should inspect what remains: in this example, notes.txt is still outside the commit. Try this sequence before your next focused commit.

metadata.description:
Learn how to commit only one changed file in Git by staging app.py, inspecting the staged diff, committing the index, and checking what remains.

This beginner example explains the difference between the working tree, staging area, and commit using git status, git add, git diff --cached, and git commit.
